title: Ramayana Is Heading to Hall H. India's $400 Million Epic Eyes a San Diego Comic-Con Trailer Drop in July.
excerpt: Between Avengers: Doomsday and Dune 3, Ranbir Kapoor's Lord Rama may unveil his trailer to the world. India isn't asking for a seat anymore — it's bringing its own epic.
body:
Picture it: July 24, 2026. Hall H at the San Diego Convention Center — the holiest room in global fan culture, where *Avengers* casts get standing ovations and grown adults weep over teaser drops. The lights go down. And onto the screen, between *Avengers: Doomsday* and *Dune 3*, comes a bow, a tilak, and a long-haired warrior-prince stepping out of an Indian epic that's older than every franchise in that room combined. If the plan holds, **Ramayana** — Nitesh Tiwari's reported ₹4,000-crore, two-part retelling — will unveil its first trailer not in Mumbai, but in California, in front of the world.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=-pcsr8Qg6Rs</youtube>

Let that sink in. India has made expensive films before. India has made global films before. But India has never walked into the lion's den of Hollywood fandom and planted its flag quite like this. According to reports from Mid-Day and others, producer **Namit Malhotra** and director **Nitesh Tiwari** have been in advanced talks with Comic-Con organizers, with the convention running July 23–26. The pitch, in the words of an industry source, is audacious in the best way:

> "Comic-Con gives it a global platform. The idea is to present the mythological drama not just as an Indian epic, but as a cinematic spectacle to the world." — industry source via Mid-Day

This isn't a vanity play. It's the culmination of a deliberate, year-long international rollout. The team has already screened footage at **CinemaCon** in the US, where Malhotra and **Yash** presented to exhibitors and walked away with encouraging feedback. There was a focus-group screening in Los Angeles that reportedly impressed a diverse, non-Indian audience. There's even chatter that the trailer could be attached to US theatrical screenings of Christopher Nolan's *The Odyssey* — a piece of counter-programming so bold it borders on cheeky. Mythology meeting mythology.

The cast reads like a coronation. **Ranbir Kapoor** plays Lord Rama — a role he initially refused, intimidated by its weight, until fatherhood reportedly shifted something in him. He's confirmed he's pulling double duty as both Rama and Parashurama. **Sai Pallavi**, the most quietly luminous actor of her generation, is Sita. **Yash**, the KGF juggernaut whose first look as Ravana fans are practically frothing for, anchors the darkness. **Sunny Deol** as Hanuman, **Ravie Dubey** as Lakshman, and an ensemble that reportedly stretches to Arun Govil, Kunal Kapoor, Lara Dutta, Rakul Preet Singh, and more. Both parts together are said to run over six hours. The first lands around Diwali 2026 — with reports suggesting a possible prepone to October 30 to milk the festive window — and the second follows on Diwali 2027.

Then there's the sound of it. Two Academy Award winners, **A.R. Rahman** and **Hans Zimmer**, sharing a score — and a planned October live musical event to show it off. Read that twice. The man who scored *Slumdog Millionaire* and the man who scored *Dune*, building the sonic architecture of the Ramayana together. The visual effects, handled by DNEG (the studio behind *Inception* and *Interstellar*), are reportedly getting a significant upgrade from the teaser visuals — Malhotra's own Prime Focus owns DNEG, which is precisely why this film can dream at this scale.

Not everything has been smooth. When set photos of Ranbir's long-haired Rama avatar leaked, the internet did what the internet does — some praised the serenity, others mocked the wig. ("All that budget and they couldn't arrange a decent-looking wig?" went one viral Reddit jab.) Malhotra has handled the noise with unusual grace, calling the audience reaction "overwhelming, inspiring, and humbling" and promising the team is "listening closely." Even **Dipika Chikhlia** — the original Sita from Ramanand Sagar's 1987 series, the Sita etched into a billion memories — gave the teaser her blessing: "Bahut rich lag raha hai. Unhone bahut achhe se banaya hai."

**For the diaspora, this is the whole point.** Comic-Con isn't being courted for Indian eyeballs — those are guaranteed. It's being courted for the second-generation kid in Houston who grew up on Marvel but heard the Ramayana only at bedtime, for the non-Indian friend who might finally see this story as cinema rather than curiosity. If Ramayana stands shoulder-to-shoulder with *Doomsday* and *Dune* in Hall H and holds the room, it changes what Indian cinema is allowed to aspire to on the world stage.

It's still reported, not confirmed — the makers haven't issued an official word, and Comic-Con plans have a way of shifting. But the ambition is unmistakable, and frankly, intoxicating. India isn't asking for a seat at the table anymore. It's bringing its own epic, four millennia in the making, and setting it down in the middle of the room. July can't come fast enough.
